question: A team proposes deriving a customer tenure feature for a churn model by subtracting each customer's signup date from today's date, recomputed automatically every time the model runs in production. What should the project manager check?
option_a: That tenure is measured as of the prediction point in training records and at production scoring time
option_b: That signup dates are stored in a date type rather than as text strings
option_c: That the tenure feature is expressed in days rather than in months
option_d: That customers with no recorded signup date are excluded from the dataset before training begins
explanation: Tenure must be measured as of the prediction point, both in historical training records and at scoring time.
explanation_a: In training, tenure should be measured as of the moment each historical outcome occurred; in production it is measured at the point of scoring. If the historical records are instead computed against today's date, the feature carries a different meaning in each setting and the learned relationship no longer holds.
explanation_b: Date typing prevents parsing errors and is worth confirming. It is a data hygiene point rather than the semantic trap in this derivation.
explanation_c: Days or months is a granularity choice with little consequence, since one converts to the other. It does not affect correctness.
explanation_d: Handling customers with no signup date is a necessary decision either way. It is a completeness question separate from the reference-point issue.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team reports a model at ninety-one per cent accuracy, measured on the records it was trained on. The team has not scored the model on any data it did not see during training, and proposes to put the figure to the steering group as evidence of the performance expected once the model is in use. What should the project manager require?
option_a: That the figure be reported with a note explaining it was measured on the training records
option_b: A score on held-out data before that claim is put to the steering group
option_c: That the team retrain the model until training accuracy reaches at least ninety-five per cent
option_d: That precision and recall be calculated alongside accuracy on the same training records
explanation: Performance measured on training records shows what a model retained, not what it will do on new cases.
explanation_a: Labelling the figure correctly is honest and worth doing. It does not turn a training score into evidence of how the model will perform in use, which is the claim being made.
explanation_b: A model can reproduce its training records closely and still fail on new ones. Only a score on data held back from training supports a claim about expected performance in use.
explanation_c: Pushing training accuracy higher moves in the wrong direction, since it can indicate the model is fitting the training records ever more closely.
explanation_d: Additional measures on the same records share the same defect. They describe the training data rather than future performance.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team is splitting data for a classifier in which one outcome accounts for about three per cent of records. A random split leaves the test set with very few examples of that outcome, and the measured performance on it varies substantially between runs. The dataset is large enough that preserving the three per cent proportion would place an adequate number of those records in the test set. What splitting approach should the project manager expect?
option_a: A larger test set, so that the rare outcome appears in it often enough to be measured reliably
option_b: Removal of the rare outcome from the test set, so the measured score is not distorted by so few cases
option_c: A stratified split, preserving the proportion of each outcome in every set
option_d: Duplication of the rare records until they make up an equal share of the test set
explanation: Preserving each class's proportion in every split stops the rare outcome's test count being left to chance.
explanation_a: Enlarging the test set does raise the count of rare cases, but it takes records away from training and still leaves their number to chance. Stratification addresses the cause directly.
explanation_b: Excluding the rare outcome removes exactly the behaviour most in need of evaluation. The resulting score would describe only the common case.
explanation_c: Stratification places the same three per cent share in each split. On a dataset of the size the stem describes, that yields a consistent and adequate number of rare cases rather than leaving the count to the draw.
explanation_d: Duplicating test records inflates the apparent sample without adding evidence, and makes the score depend repeatedly on the same few cases.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
topic: Training data strategy and validation design

question: A team is asked to make a screening model fair across two applicant groups. It finds that equalising the share of qualified applicants accepted in each group, and equalising the share of accepted applicants who prove qualified, cannot both be achieved given the different base rates. The team asks the project manager how to proceed.
option_a: Choose whichever definition the model satisfies more closely as it currently stands
option_b: Decide with the stakeholders which definition applies here, and record the reasoning
option_c: Report both measures without selecting between them, so stakeholders can see the full position
option_d: Adjust the data until the base rates in the two groups match, so both definitions can hold
explanation: Different fairness definitions can be mutually unattainable, so the choice must be made deliberately.
explanation_a: This lets the model's present behaviour set the standard, which reverses the order. The standard should be chosen first and the model measured against it.
explanation_b: When the definitions cannot hold together, the choice is about which harm matters more in this setting. That is a decision for accountable stakeholders, documented so it can be reviewed.
explanation_c: Transparent reporting is necessary and should happen regardless. It does not discharge the obligation to decide which standard the model must meet.
explanation_d: Altering the data to remove a real difference misrepresents the population, and the model would be tuned to a situation that does not exist.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team has spent three months on model experiments. Performance improved substantially in the first month, marginally in the second and not at all in the third. The team requests two further months, arguing that a breakthrough is still possible. What should the project manager weigh?
option_a: Whether the current model is good enough to be useful, against the cost of continuing
option_b: Whether the team has tried every algorithm that could plausibly suit this problem
option_c: Whether two months matches the time already spent, so the investment is balanced
option_d: Whether the sponsor is willing to fund two further months of the team's time
explanation: A flattening improvement curve is evidence about expected return, and a stopping rule should reflect it.
explanation_a: The pattern of gains suggests further effort will return little. The decision turns on whether what exists now delivers value, not on whether a breakthrough remains conceivable.
explanation_b: Exhausting the options is not a stopping rule, since the list is effectively open-ended. It would justify indefinite continuation.
explanation_c: Time already spent is not recoverable and should not shape the decision. Only the expected return on further effort is relevant.
explanation_d: Willingness to fund is necessary to proceed but does not establish that proceeding is worthwhile.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team must classify incoming support tickets into a small set of categories. One member proposes adapting a general-purpose language model; another proposes training a classifier on the organisation's own labelled ticket history. The project manager is asked to decide how the options should be compared.
option_a: Choose the general-purpose model, as it has seen far more text than the organisation holds
option_b: Choose the in-house classifier, as a model built on the organisation's own tickets always fits better
option_c: Combine both approaches so that the strengths of each one are retained
option_d: Evaluate both approaches against the same held-out tickets and the same agreed success measure
explanation: Competing approaches are chosen on evidence against the same task, not on the reputation of the method.
explanation_a: Broad pretraining is an advantage on general language, but the task is this organisation's own categories. Whether that advantage carries over is exactly what the comparison is meant to establish.
explanation_b: Matching the organisation's categories may help, but it does not guarantee better performance. A small or inconsistent ticket history can still produce a weaker classifier than an adapted general model.
explanation_c: Combining methods may be worth exploring later, but it adds cost and complexity before either approach has been shown to work. The decision in front of the project manager is how to compare them.
explanation_d: Running both approaches on identical data and one agreed measure makes the comparison meaningful. Anything else compares the methods' reputations rather than their performance on this task.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team proposes a cut-off that would send roughly four hundred cases a day for manual review. The review team consists of six people who can each assess about twenty cases a day. The team argues the cut-off is correct because it maximises the number of genuine cases caught. What should the project manager conclude?
option_a: The cut-off is correct, since catching the greatest number of genuine cases is the model's purpose
option_b: The review team should be expanded until it can assess every case the model flags
option_c: A cut-off producing more cases than can be reviewed will leave most of them unactioned
option_d: The cases should be reviewed in the order they arrive so none of them waits unduly long
explanation: A cut-off that exceeds the capacity to act on its output delivers less than one that fits within it.
explanation_a: The purpose is acting on genuine cases, not flagging them. Flags that no one can assess do not produce the intended outcome.
explanation_b: Expanding the team may be one option to put to the sponsor. It is a resourcing proposal rather than the conclusion to draw about the cut-off as it stands.
explanation_c: Around a hundred and twenty cases a day can be assessed. The rest queue or lapse, so the genuine cases in that remainder are caught on paper but not in practice.
explanation_d: Arrival order distributes the delay but does not create capacity. The same proportion of cases still goes unassessed.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team reports that its model classifies ninety-six per cent of training records correctly but only sixty-one per cent of the held-out test records. The team is pleased with the training figure. What does the gap between the two indicate?
option_a: The test set must contain records that are harder than those used for training
option_b: The model has learned the training records rather than the underlying pattern
option_c: The model needs more training rounds to bring the test figure up to the training figure
option_d: The training figure is the one to report, since it rests on far more records than the test figure
explanation: A large gap between training and held-out performance is evidence the model has fitted its training set.
explanation_a: A random split gives no reason to expect the test records to be systematically harder than the training records. A gap of this size is more consistent with the model than with an unlucky draw.
explanation_b: Detail specific to the training records does not recur in new data. The model reproduces what it memorised, which is why performance falls away on records it has not seen.
explanation_c: Continuing to train does not by itself establish that held-out performance will catch up. Where the model is already fitting training detail, further training can widen the gap instead.
explanation_d: Sample size does not make a training score informative. It measures material the model has already seen.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team reports unusually strong test performance on a document classification model. Investigation shows the source system had recorded many documents twice, and the random split placed copies of the same document in both the training and the test set. What does this mean for the reported score?
option_a: The score partly measures documents the model already saw during training
option_b: The score is valid, because duplicate documents are genuine records that occur in the real data
option_c: The score is too low, because duplicated documents take up places that other documents could have filled
option_d: The duplicates should be left in place and the model retrained with a smaller training set
explanation: A test record the model has already seen in training measures recall of that record, not generalisation.
explanation_a: For every duplicated document the model is being asked about material it has already learned. Those cases inflate the score without saying anything about unseen documents.
explanation_b: Duplicates may well occur in the source system, but that does not make them valid test cases here. The test set must contain material the model has not been trained on.
explanation_c: The direction is wrong. Seeing the same document in training makes the test easier, so the score is inflated rather than depressed.
explanation_d: Shrinking the training set does not separate the copies. The duplicates would still straddle the split and the score would still be inflated.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team encodes two categorical fields for a pricing model. One records a service tier as standard, priority or express; the other records the handling depot, of which there are nine with no inherent ordering. The team applies the same numeric encoding to both. What problem does this create?
option_a: The service tier field is given an order that its three levels do not carry
option_b: Nine depots is too many distinct values for a categorical field to be usable
option_c: The depot field is given an order and a spacing that it does not actually have
option_d: Both fields need numbers, so one consistent encoding across them is correct
explanation: Encoding an unordered category as a number asserts an ordering and spacing the data does not have.
explanation_a: The tiers do carry a natural progression from standard through priority to express, so a numeric encoding is defensible there. The unordered field is the one that is misrepresented.
explanation_b: Nine categories is a modest number and presents no particular difficulty. The issue is the kind of encoding applied, not the count of categories.
explanation_c: Numbering the depots implies that depot seven sits between six and eight in some meaningful sense. No such relationship exists, so the model is fed a structure that is not real.
explanation_d: Consistency is not the goal. The encoding has to match the nature of each field, and applying one scheme to fields of different kinds is what causes the problem.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team is predicting how many days a repair will take. It reports that the model is correct eighty-two per cent of the time. The project manager notes that the quantity being predicted is a number of days rather than a category. What is wrong with the way performance has been reported?
option_a: A numeric prediction should be judged by the size of its error, not by exact matches
option_b: Eighty-two per cent is too low a figure to support deploying a repair duration model
option_c: The model should predict a range of days rather than a single number of days
option_d: Accuracy should have been reported separately for each type of repair in the dataset
explanation: A prediction of a quantity is judged by how far it lands from the truth, not by whether it is exactly right.
explanation_a: Treating a predicted duration as right or wrong throws away how wrong it was. A forecast one day out and one thirty days out are very different, and the reported figure cannot tell them apart.
explanation_b: Whether a level of performance is adequate depends on the use. The reporting problem stands regardless of whether the number is high or low.
explanation_c: Predicting an interval can be genuinely useful for planning. It is a change to what the model outputs and does not fix how the current output is being scored.
explanation_d: Breaking results down by repair type is worthwhile analysis. It does not address the use of an exact-match measure for a numeric prediction.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team proposes generating synthetic records to enlarge a small training set for a credit risk model, arguing that the real data will take another two quarters to accumulate. The sponsor is willing to fund the tooling. What should the project manager require the team to establish?
option_a: That synthetic records can be produced faster than real records are collected
option_b: That synthetic records are stored separately from real records in the warehouse
option_c: That synthetic records preserve the relationships and variation relevant to the prediction task
option_d: That synthetic records are generated by a vendor tool rather than in-house code
explanation: Synthetic data is only useful if it carries the structure the model needs to learn.
explanation_a: Generation speed is an advantage of synthesis and is not the binding constraint here. Producing unhelpful records quickly does not advance the model.
explanation_b: Keeping synthetic and real records distinguishable is sound data management and supports later evaluation. Storage separation does not make the synthetic data fit for training.
explanation_c: The value of synthetic records depends on whether they preserve the relationships and variation relevant to the prediction task. Their usefulness should then be checked against real held-out data.
explanation_d: Vendor tooling may bring maturity and validation features worth having. Provenance of the generator is not what determines whether the output is faithful.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
topic: Training data strategy and validation design

question: An agreed requirement for a maintenance prioritisation model states that a supervisor must be able to see why a job was ranked where it was. At the evaluation review the team presents accuracy figures and a ranked list, but the model produces no case-level reasoning. What is missing before the model can pass evaluation?
option_a: A training session explaining how the model was built and which algorithm it uses
option_b: A higher overall accuracy figure, so supervisors have more reason to trust the ranking
option_c: A process allowing supervisors to override any recommendation they disagree with
option_d: Evidence that the model can produce the case-level reasoning the requirement specifies
explanation: A model is evaluated against every agreed requirement, not only against its performance figures.
explanation_a: Explaining the method in general does not demonstrate that the model can give a reason for an individual ranking, which is what the agreed requirement specifies.
explanation_b: A higher figure speaks to how often the ranking is right, not to whether a supervisor can see why a job was ranked where it was. The requirement would remain unevidenced.
explanation_c: An override route lets a supervisor reject a ranking without understanding it. It does not supply the case-level reasoning the requirement calls for.
explanation_d: The requirement forms part of what the model is evaluated against. Performance figures do not show it is met, so until case-level reasoning is demonstrated the model has not passed evaluation.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A sponsor asks the project manager to commit to a schedule in which model performance improves by a set amount in each of the next four months. The team has already made the gains available from straightforward changes. What should the project manager explain?
option_a: Improvement will continue at a steady rate provided the team's resourcing is maintained at its current level
option_b: Further gains are uncertain in size and timing, so they cannot be scheduled as fixed increments
option_c: The schedule can be met if the team is permitted to change the measure used to report performance
option_d: Performance targets should be set only after the model has been deployed and observed in use
explanation: Model improvement is investigative work, so equal gains cannot be committed to on a fixed schedule.
explanation_a: Resourcing supports the work but does not make the results regular. Effort and improvement are not proportional in investigative work.
explanation_b: Each experiment may or may not yield an improvement. Once the straightforward gains are taken, remaining progress depends on findings that cannot be committed to in advance.
explanation_c: Changing the measure to produce a rising number reports progress that has not occurred. It would mislead the sponsor.
explanation_d: Targets are needed before deployment to decide whether to deploy at all. Deferring them removes the basis for that decision.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team is beginning model development for a demand forecasting problem and proposes moving straight to a complex architecture, on the grounds that the business expects a sophisticated solution. The project manager asks what the results will be compared against. What should the project manager require first?
option_a: A sponsor commitment to fund the complex architecture through to deployment
option_b: A written statement of the intended architecture and the libraries it depends on
option_c: An estimate of the computing time the architecture will need during training
option_d: A simple baseline, so any gain from the complex approach can be measured against it
explanation: Without a simple reference point, a complex model's score cannot be shown to be worth its cost.
explanation_a: Funding certainty helps planning but says nothing about whether the complex approach performs better than a simple one. The comparison question the project manager raised would remain unanswered.
explanation_b: Recording the intended architecture is reasonable documentation. It does not establish a reference point against which the resulting model's performance can be judged.
explanation_c: Compute cost is worth knowing, but it measures what the approach consumes rather than what it delivers. It provides no comparison for the model's accuracy.
explanation_d: A baseline establishes what performance is achievable cheaply. Only the margin above it shows what the complex model contributes, which is what justifies its cost and its ongoing maintenance.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: Before a fraud detection model goes live, the project manager wants the cut-off set deliberately rather than by default. The team asks what information is needed from the business to make that decision. Select two.
option_a: The algorithm the team used to produce the fraud scores
option_b: The relative cost of a missed fraud and a wrongly flagged transaction
option_c: The share of transactions that were fraudulent in each of the last three years
option_d: The number of flagged cases the review team can handle in a day
explanation: Setting a cut-off requires knowing what each error costs and how much review capacity exists.
explanation_a: The method behind the scores does not determine where the cut-off belongs. The same cut-off question arises whatever algorithm produced them.
explanation_b: The cut-off balances the two errors, so their relative cost sets where the balance should fall. Without it the choice has no basis beyond convention.
explanation_c: Historical prevalence is useful background for interpreting the scores. It does not by itself say what balance of errors the business should accept.
explanation_d: A cut-off that flags more cases than the team can review produces a backlog, and the unreviewed cases receive no action. Capacity puts a practical ceiling on the choice.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
option_e: The total number of features the model uses to generate each score
explanation_e: Feature count describes the model's construction and has no bearing on where the decision boundary should sit.

question: A team's model scores poorly on both the training data and the held-out data, at levels close to what a simple guess would achieve. Training has been run to convergence and the usual optimisation settings have been tried without effect. The team proposes collecting substantially more records of the same kind. What should the project manager consider first?
option_a: Whether the held-out set is large enough for the reported score to be stable
option_b: Whether the team has trained for long enough for performance to settle
option_c: Whether the model and its features can represent the relationship at all
option_d: Whether the additional records can be collected within the schedule the sponsor agreed
explanation: Where a converged model underperforms on its own training data, capacity or features are the constraint.
explanation_a: Test set size affects how precisely performance is measured. It does not explain a model that also fails on its training data.
explanation_b: The stem establishes that training has been run to convergence, so duration has already been ruled out as the explanation.
explanation_c: With training converged, weak performance on the records the model was fitted to points at the model or the feature representation rather than the amount of data. More records of the same kind are unlikely to address that.
explanation_d: Feasibility of collection matters only once more data is established as the remedy, which it has not been.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team is building a model to predict readmission from patient records. Many patients appear several times in the dataset, once per admission. The evaluation is required to estimate how the model will perform for patients not represented in the training data. The team splits the records at random, so a given patient's admissions can fall on both sides of the split. What risk does this create?
option_a: The model can recognise individual patients rather than learn the pattern behind readmission
option_b: Patients with several admissions will be weighted more heavily than patients with only one
option_c: The test set will contain fewer distinct patients than the training set, making it less representative
option_d: Admissions for the same patient may have been recorded in different formats over time
explanation: Where the objective is performance on unseen entities, the split must separate entities rather than records.
explanation_a: Admissions for one patient share many characteristics. With the same patient on both sides, the model can succeed by matching a familiar patient, which is precisely what the stated evaluation objective excludes.
explanation_b: Repeated records do give frequent patients more influence during training, which is worth managing. It is a separate issue from the split placing one patient on both sides.
explanation_c: The counts follow from the proportions of the split and are not the problem. The problem is that the same patient appears in both sets.
explanation_d: Inconsistent recording is a data quality matter to be checked. It is unrelated to how the split was drawn.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team is preparing a feature set in which one field records an age in years and another records an annual amount that runs into the hundreds of thousands. The team plans to use a method that is sensitive to the relative scale of its inputs. What preparation step does this call for?
option_a: Removing the larger-valued field, since it would otherwise overwhelm the other
option_b: Placing both fields on a comparable scale before training begins
option_c: Rounding the larger values so both fields hold a similar number of digits
option_d: Recording both fields as text so the method does not read them as quantities
explanation: Scale-sensitive methods treat a large-valued field as more important simply because its numbers are bigger.
explanation_a: Dropping the field discards information that may be genuinely predictive. The problem is the difference in scale, which rescaling addresses without losing the field.
explanation_b: Where a method measures distances or weights inputs by magnitude, the field with larger numbers dominates. Rescaling puts the fields on comparable footing so each contributes on its merits.
explanation_c: Rounding reduces precision without reliably equalising scale, and it destroys detail in the larger field. It is not a substitute for a proper rescaling step.
explanation_d: Storing numbers as text prevents the method from using their magnitude at all, which removes real information. The aim is comparable scale, not the loss of numeric meaning.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team presents a confusion matrix for a classifier that identifies faulty parts. The project manager wants to know how often a part the model flagged as faulty actually turned out to be faulty, because every flagged part is pulled off the line for inspection. Which measure answers that question?
option_a: Recall, the share of genuinely faulty parts that the model managed to flag
option_b: Precision, the share of flagged parts that were genuinely faulty
option_c: Overall accuracy, the share of all parts the model classified correctly
option_d: Specificity, the share of sound parts that the model correctly left unflagged
explanation: Precision describes how often a positive prediction is correct, which matters when every false positive triggers unnecessary inspection.
explanation_a: Recall answers the complementary question of how many faults were caught. It says nothing about how many flagged parts turn out to be sound.
explanation_b: Precision looks only at the cases the model flagged and asks how many were right. That directly answers how often a flagged part actually proves faulty; combined with flagged volume, it can also help quantify inspection effort spent on sound parts.
explanation_c: Accuracy pools flagged and unflagged parts together. A model can score well on it while most of its flags are wrong, particularly when faults are uncommon.
explanation_d: Specificity describes behaviour on sound parts across the whole line. It does not isolate the flagged group that inspection actually acts on.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team splits its data into a training set, a validation set and a test set. A stakeholder asks why two separate held-out sets are needed when one would be simpler to manage. What is the reason for keeping them separate?
option_a: The validation set guides development choices, so an untouched test set gives the final independent estimate
option_b: The validation set checks the training data quality and the test set checks the model
option_c: Two held-out sets allow the team to report two accuracy figures to the stakeholders
option_d: The validation set is used during training and the test set after the model is deployed
explanation: A set used to make development choices can no longer provide an independent estimate of performance.
explanation_a: Each time the validation set informs a decision, the model is shaped a little to suit it. A set that played no part in those decisions provides the independent estimate of behaviour on new data.
explanation_b: Checking data quality is a separate purpose from the roles of the validation and test sets. The validation set guides development choices, while the untouched test set provides the final independent estimate.
explanation_c: Reporting two numbers is a consequence, not a purpose. The reason for the separation is that only one of them is an independent estimate.
explanation_d: The test set is used before deployment to support the go-live decision. Holding it until after deployment would leave that decision unevidenced.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
topic: Training data strategy and validation design

question: A team removes an applicant's recorded gender from a credit model's inputs and reports that the model can no longer discriminate on that basis. The remaining features include occupation, purchasing categories and the applicant's employment history. What should the project manager raise?
option_a: Removing the field will reduce the model's accuracy and should therefore be reconsidered
option_b: The field should be retained so the model can be tested for differences between groups
option_c: Remaining features may carry the same information, so the pattern can persist
option_d: The remaining features should be reduced in number until none of them relates to the removed field
explanation: Removing an attribute does not remove it from the model if other fields carry the same information.
explanation_a: Accuracy may or may not fall, and would not justify reinstating the field here. The concern is whether removal achieved what was claimed.
explanation_b: Group information is needed to evaluate outcomes, but it can be held for evaluation without being used as a model input. The two uses are separable.
explanation_c: Occupation, purchasing patterns and other remaining features may carry information correlated with the removed attribute. The model can reconstruct it in effect, so outcomes must still be examined by group.
explanation_d: Very many features relate weakly to such an attribute, so this would strip the model of most of its inputs while still not guaranteeing the outcome.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: Evaluation shows a model falls well short of the agreed performance level, and the team's analysis attributes this mainly to gaps and inconsistencies in the input data rather than to the modelling approach. The sponsor asks what happens next. What should the project manager advise?
option_a: Continue with further modelling approaches, since one of them may overcome the data limitations
option_b: Lower the agreed performance level to one the current model can meet
option_c: Deploy the model to a small group of users so real-world evidence can be gathered
option_d: Return to the data work before further modelling is attempted
explanation: An evaluation result can send a project back to an earlier phase rather than onward to the next.
explanation_a: Some approaches tolerate imperfect data better than others, but none can supply information the data does not contain. This spends effort where the constraint is not.
explanation_b: Moving the standard to fit the result removes the purpose of setting it. The level was chosen to reflect what the business needs.
explanation_c: Releasing a model known to fall short exposes users to poor outcomes, and the cause is already understood well enough to act on.
explanation_d: The evidence points at the data, so continuing to try modelling approaches would address the wrong constraint. Revisiting an earlier phase is a normal outcome of evaluation, not a failure.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team proposes a deep neural network for a problem with roughly eight hundred labelled records and twelve input fields. The sponsor is impressed by the proposal. The project manager asks the team to justify the choice against a simpler statistical model. What is the central concern?
option_a: Neural networks need input fields converted into images before training on tabular data
option_b: A high-capacity model relative to the available evidence carries a greater overfitting risk
option_c: Twelve input fields is too few for any model to predict usefully on this problem
option_d: No single accuracy figure can be reported to the sponsor for a neural network
explanation: Additional model capacity has to earn its place against a simpler baseline on held-out performance.
explanation_a: Neural networks accept tabular numeric input directly. No conversion into images is involved, so this misstates how the method works.
explanation_b: The proposed approach has enough flexibility to fit patterns specific to eight hundred records. That makes evidence necessary that its additional complexity improves held-out performance over the simpler model.
explanation_c: Twelve fields can be perfectly adequate. The difficulty here is the number of records relative to the model's flexibility, not the number of fields.
explanation_d: A neural network can be scored with the same measures as any other classifier. Reporting is not the constraint.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team lowers the score at which a collections model refers an account for intervention, so that more at-risk accounts are caught. The project manager is asked what else will change as a result. What should be expected?
option_a: The model will become more accurate on both the at-risk and the sound accounts
option_b: The proportion of referred accounts that genuinely need intervention will rise
option_c: The model will need to be retrained before the change to the cut-off takes effect
option_d: More accounts in total will be referred for intervention
explanation: Lowering a decision threshold admits every case the higher threshold admitted, so the number acted on rises.
explanation_a: A cut-off change trades performance between the two groups rather than improving both. Gains on at-risk accounts come at the expense of sound ones.
explanation_b: Accounts admitted by the lower bar carry weaker evidence of risk than those already referred, so the share of referrals that prove justified tends to fall rather than rise.
explanation_c: A cut-off is applied to scores the existing model already produces. No retraining is required to change it.
explanation_d: A lower bar admits every account the higher bar admitted, plus those scoring between the two. The referral count therefore rises, and the accounts added carry weaker evidence of risk.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team reports that model A scored two points higher than model B on a held-out set of ninety records, and recommends model A on that basis. The project manager notes that a difference of two points on this set corresponds to about two records. What should be concluded?
option_a: The two-point difference alone is not sufficient evidence that model A is better
option_b: Model A should be selected, since it scored higher and a decision has to be made
option_c: Model B should be selected, because the smaller measured difference suggests it is more stable
option_d: The models should be combined, since neither has been shown to be better than the other
explanation: A small-sample difference is not evidence of a better model until its uncertainty has been assessed.
explanation_a: On ninety records a two-record difference is small relative to the uncertainty in each estimate. Establishing a real difference calls for repeated or paired evaluation, or an interval around each score.
explanation_b: A decision does have to be made, but it should rest on evidence that distinguishes the options. Further evaluation, or another criterion, is the appropriate route.
explanation_c: Nothing in the comparison speaks to stability. A lower score does not indicate more consistent behaviour.
explanation_d: Combining them adds complexity without addressing the question. Indistinguishable performance is a reason to look further, not to merge.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team building a churn model presents its feature list to the project manager. One field records whether the customer has been assigned to the retention outreach team, and the team notes it is among the strongest predictors found so far. The model is intended to score customers before any retention assignment is made. What concern should the project manager raise?
option_a: The field may be missing for customers who joined most recently
option_b: The field may be stored as a flag rather than as a descriptive category
option_c: The field is created after the intended scoring point, so it will not be available with the same meaning
option_d: The field may be refreshed on a slower cycle than the other customer attributes in the dataset
explanation: A feature created after the model's intended scoring point will not be available when the prediction is required.
explanation_a: Recent joiners having sparser history is a routine completeness pattern. It is a data gap rather than the structural problem with this feature.
explanation_b: Storage as a flag or a category is an encoding choice that is easily handled. Representation is not the issue.
explanation_c: The model is intended to score customers before any retention assignment exists, so the field will not carry the same value or meaning at that point. Its strength in training reflects information recorded after the scoring point rather than available at it.
explanation_d: Differing refresh cadence affects timeliness across fields. It does not explain why this particular field is unsafe to use.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team preparing features for a maintenance prediction model has worked only from the recorded fields, without consulting the engineers who operate the equipment. The project manager notices that no feature reflects how the machines are actually run. What is the value of involving those engineers?
option_a: They can confirm the recorded fields use correct data types and units throughout
option_b: They can approve the feature set so the modelling work has operational sign-off
option_c: They can name operating conditions worth deriving that the raw fields do not record
option_d: They can say which machine learning algorithm suits equipment data of this kind
explanation: Operational knowledge identifies quantities worth deriving that the raw records do not contain.
explanation_a: Checking types and units is worthwhile data preparation work, and engineers may help. It verifies the existing fields rather than identifying quantities the feature set is missing.
explanation_b: Sign-off records agreement. It does not add the operating knowledge that would improve which features exist in the first place.
explanation_c: People who run the equipment know which combinations of readings signal trouble. Those conditions can often be computed from existing fields once someone names them, and are missed otherwise.
explanation_d: Algorithm selection is not where their expertise lies. Their contribution is knowledge of the equipment, not of modelling methods.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team reports that raising a fraud model's recall from sixty to eighty per cent caused its precision to fall from seventy to forty-five per cent. A stakeholder asks whether the change is an improvement. What should the project manager say determines the answer?
option_a: Whether the sum of precision and recall is higher after the change than it was before
option_b: What a missed fraud costs compared with a review of a legitimate case
option_c: Whether the model's overall accuracy also improved when the change was made
option_d: Whether the recall figure now exceeds the precision figure by a clear margin
explanation: Whether a precision and recall trade is worth making depends on what each kind of error costs.
explanation_a: Adding the two measures treats the errors as interchangeable. They are not, and the sum has no meaning in terms of what the organisation loses.
explanation_b: The trade moves error from one type to the other. Only the relative consequences of a missed fraud and a review of a legitimate case can establish whether the new balance is preferable.
explanation_c: Overall accuracy combines both error types into a single figure and can move very little when either measure changes. It cannot arbitrate a trade between them.
explanation_d: There is no general principle that recall should exceed precision. Which matters more depends entirely on the costs involved.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: Over several weeks a team has adjusted its model many times, checking the test set after each change and keeping whichever adjustments raised the test score. The final test accuracy is the highest achieved. The project manager is asked to sign off on that figure as the expected production performance. What is the concern?
option_a: The team should have kept the adjustments that lowered the test score as well, for completeness
option_b: The test accuracy is reliable, since every adjustment was measured on the same held-out records throughout
option_c: Test accuracy alone is never sufficient, so precision and recall should also be reported
option_d: Repeated tuning against the test set has made its score an optimistic estimate
explanation: A held-out set consulted repeatedly during tuning stops being held out and starts being fitted.
explanation_a: Retaining changes that hurt performance would not improve the estimate. The problem lies in using the test set to make the choices at all.
explanation_b: Using the same records consistently is exactly what allows the fitting to accumulate. Consistency makes the optimism systematic rather than removing it.
explanation_c: Reporting further measures is good practice, and worth doing. Those measures would be inflated by the same repeated tuning, so it does not resolve the concern.
explanation_d: Each decision taken because it improved the test score fits the model a little more closely to those particular records. The final figure reflects that fitting as well as genuine capability.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
topic: Training data strategy and validation design

question: A team has built an assistant on a general-purpose language model to answer staff questions from the organisation's policy documents. Before release, the project manager wants evidence about answers that sound authoritative but are not supported by those documents. Select two.
option_a: Testing on questions whose correct answers are known and verified against the policies
option_b: Confirming that the assistant responds in fluent and professional language
option_c: Checking whether cited passages actually support the claims in sampled answers
option_d: Measuring the average time the assistant takes to return an answer
explanation: Confident wording, and the presence of a citation, are not evidence that an answer is supported.
explanation_a: A known-answer set is what makes an unsupported answer visible. Without it there is no basis for saying whether the assistant is accurate on the policies.
explanation_b: Fluency is what makes an unsupported answer convincing in the first place. It offers no evidence about correctness.
explanation_c: A citation can be produced that does not support the claim it is attached to. Verifying sampled answers against the passages they cite is what tests grounding rather than its appearance.
explanation_d: Response time is a service quality measure. It carries no information about whether answers are supported.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
option_e: Counting the number of policy documents loaded into the assistant
explanation_e: The size of the document set says nothing about whether answers drawn from it are accurate.

question: A team has run dozens of model variants over several weeks. Asked to reproduce the result the sponsor was shown a month ago, the team cannot establish which data extract, feature set and settings produced it. What practice would have prevented this?
option_a: Recording the data version, feature set and settings with every run
option_b: Running fewer variants, so the team can keep track of what it has tried
option_c: Keeping the final model's code in version control so it can be inspected later
option_d: Presenting results to the sponsor only once the final model has been selected
explanation: A result is only defensible if the inputs and settings that produced it were recorded with it.
explanation_a: A result is reproducible only when everything that fed it is captured alongside it. Without that record the team has a number it cannot stand behind or return to.
explanation_b: Limiting experimentation restricts the search for a good model. The problem is the absence of records, not the number of runs.
explanation_c: Code alone does not reproduce a result. The data extract and settings used at the time are equally necessary.
explanation_d: Withholding interim results reduces visibility for the sponsor and would not have made the earlier figure reproducible.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team reports that it evaluated five candidate algorithms and selected the best performer. On review, the project manager finds that each algorithm was assessed on a different random split of the data, because team members worked independently. What is the consequence for the selection?
option_a: It is sound provided each member applied the same random splitting procedure
option_b: It is sound because several splits test the candidates under more varied conditions
option_c: The comparison is confounded, because each model was evaluated on different cases
option_d: It is unreliable because five candidates is too few to find the strongest algorithm
explanation: A comparison isolates the model choice only when every candidate is evaluated on the same cases.
explanation_a: Using the same procedure does not produce the same split. Different splits yield different test cases, so the comparison remains confounded.
explanation_b: Varied conditions are useful when every candidate faces the same variation. Here each candidate faced different conditions, so the variation confounds the comparison instead of strengthening it.
explanation_c: Each split contains its own mix of records, so a score reflects both the algorithm and the cases it was scored on. Candidates must be evaluated on the same held-out set, or the same cross-validation folds, to isolate the effect of the model choice.
explanation_d: The number of candidates is not the defect. Even two candidates would be uncomparable if each were scored on a different split.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team deploys a classifier using the cut-off of one half that its library applies by default, and describes this as the standard setting. The project manager asks what the setting means for the business. The team cannot say. What is the underlying problem?
option_a: The default is only valid for models whose output is a probability rather than a raw score
option_b: The default should be changed to whichever value produces the highest recall on the test set
option_c: The team should adopt the cut-off used by the previous rules-based process for consistency
option_d: A library default encodes no judgement about the consequences of acting
explanation: A default cut-off is a software convention, not a decision about what the organisation should act on.
explanation_a: The type of output affects how a cut-off is expressed but not whether the default suits the decision. A probability default is just as arbitrary.
explanation_b: Maximising recall alone drives the cut-off towards flagging everything. That is a different arbitrary choice, not a considered one.
explanation_c: The previous process produced different quantities, so its threshold does not transfer. Consistency of number is not consistency of meaning.
explanation_d: The cut-off determines who is acted on and who is not. That is a business decision about acceptable error, and a library has no knowledge of the costs involved.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A model performs well in testing on complete, well-formed records. In production, a share of incoming records will be missing one or two fields, and some free-text fields will contain abbreviations that did not appear during development. What should the project manager require before deployment?
option_a: Evaluation on records that reproduce the gaps and variations production will deliver
option_b: A rule that rejects any incoming record that is not complete and well formed
option_c: A larger training set, so the model encounters more variation during its training
option_d: Confirmation from the source systems that they will supply complete records in future
explanation: A model must be evaluated against the imperfect inputs it will actually receive, not only clean ones.
explanation_a: Testing only on clean records leaves the behaviour on realistic inputs unknown. The model may degrade sharply, fail outright, or produce confident but wrong outputs.
explanation_b: Rejecting imperfect records shifts the problem to whoever must handle the rejects, and may exclude a large share of genuine cases from the service.
explanation_c: More training data may help if it contains the variation concerned. The immediate requirement is to find out how the current model behaves on it.
explanation_d: Even if that commitment is honoured, it does not establish how the current model behaves on the imperfect inputs it is already expected to encounter, including the abbreviations already present.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team preparing data for an order value model computes the average order value across the entire dataset and uses that figure to fill in missing values. Once the imputation is complete, the team splits the data into training and test sets and begins modelling. What is the problem?
option_a: The average is a poor estimate of order value for most individual customers
option_b: Test set information influenced the training data through the shared average
option_c: The imputed records should have been flagged so the model can identify them
option_d: The average should have been computed separately for each product category
explanation: Preprocessing fitted across the full dataset breaks the independence of the held-out set.
explanation_a: A single average is a crude imputation and can be a weak estimate for individual records. That is a quality concern, and it exists whether or not the split ordering was wrong.
explanation_b: The average was computed over records that later became the test set, so the test set is no longer fully independent of the training data. The resulting estimate may be optimistic or otherwise biased.
explanation_c: Flagging imputed values is useful and helps the model distinguish real values from filled ones. It does not address the contamination between the two sets.
explanation_d: Category-level averages can impute better than one global figure. Refining the statistic does not stop it being fitted across the split.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team reports that three features carry very low importance scores in the trained model and proposes removing them to simplify the feature set. One of the three is a safety-related field that subject matter experts consider essential to the decision. What should the project manager establish before the removal?
option_a: Whether removing three features cuts training time enough to justify the change
option_b: Why a field the experts consider essential scores as low importance in this model
option_c: Whether the importance scores used the same method for all three features
option_d: Whether the experts can supply records in which the safety field varies more
explanation: A low importance score describes this model on this data, not the real-world relevance of the field.
explanation_a: Training time is a minor consideration at this scale and is not what makes the removal questionable. The disagreement between the score and expert judgement is the issue.
explanation_b: A low score can mean the field is genuinely uninformative, or that it is poorly recorded, rarely varies in the training period, or duplicated by another feature. Each has a different remedy.
explanation_c: Consistent calculation is a fair check, and worth confirming. It does not explain why a field the experts call essential appears unimportant.
explanation_d: Gathering more varied data may eventually help, but it presumes the cause is limited variation. The cause has not yet been established.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A model that predicts which customers will accept an offer is reported at seventy-eight per cent accuracy. The project manager finds that seventy-six per cent of customers in the data declined every offer, so a model that predicted refusal for everyone would score almost as well. What does this comparison establish?
option_a: The model is performing well, because seventy-eight per cent correct is a strong result in absolute terms
option_b: The data should be rebalanced so that acceptances and refusals appear in equal numbers
option_c: Only two percentage points of the reported figure sit above the majority-class baseline
option_d: The accuracy figure was calculated incorrectly, since it is so close to the share of refusals
explanation: A model's score is only interpretable against what the simplest available rule already achieves.
explanation_a: An absolute figure means little without a reference point. Here the reference point is almost as high, which is what the comparison was made to reveal.
explanation_b: Changing the class balance alters the problem the model is solving and the figures it produces. It does not answer whether the current model is worth anything.
explanation_c: The baseline requires no model at all, so isolating the margin above it shows what the model itself contributes. Whether a margin of that size is worth having is a business judgement.
explanation_d: The closeness is a real property of an imbalanced problem, not a sign of a calculation error.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team is forecasting weekly product demand. It creates its training and test sets by assigning weeks to each set at random across the full three-year history. The reported accuracy is high, and the team recommends deployment. What is the flaw in this evaluation?
option_a: Three years of weekly data is not enough history for a demand forecasting model to be evaluated
option_b: Weeks should be assigned to the sets in equal numbers so each set covers the same span of time
option_c: Training weeks drawn from after the test weeks let the model use later information
option_d: Demand data should be aggregated to months before a model is trained and evaluated on it
explanation: Randomly splitting a time series lets the model learn from periods that follow the ones it is scored on.
explanation_a: Around a hundred and fifty weeks is a workable series for many demand problems. The length of the history is not what makes this evaluation misleading.
explanation_b: Equal-sized sets do not fix the ordering problem. Balanced sets drawn at random still mix future and past between training and test.
explanation_c: In production the model will only ever have the past available. A random split gives it surrounding weeks from the future, so the test measures an easier task than the real one.
explanation_d: Choosing a time granularity is a modelling decision with arguments on both sides. It has no bearing on whether the split respects chronology.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
topic: Training data strategy and validation design

question: A model is approaching a deployment decision. The project manager finds that its intended use, the population it was evaluated on and the conditions under which it should not be relied upon have not been written down anywhere. The team considers this documentation to be a post-deployment task. What is the risk of deferring it?
option_a: The model may be applied outside the conditions it was evaluated for
option_b: The team will have forgotten the details of the evaluation by the time it writes them down
option_c: The deployment will be delayed while the documentation is prepared after release
option_d: Auditors will require the documentation to be rewritten in a prescribed format later on
explanation: Undocumented limits become invisible, and a model may be applied where it was not shown to work.
explanation_a: Without documented limits, downstream users may apply the model outside the population or conditions for which it was evaluated, with nothing available to tell them where it does not apply.
explanation_b: Recollection may fade, and records can be reconstructed from the evaluation artefacts. The consequential risk is misuse in the meantime.
explanation_c: Documentation written after release does not delay the release. The concern is what happens in the period without it.
explanation_d: Format requirements are a compliance detail. They do not describe what goes wrong operationally when limits are unrecorded.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A model in development is retrained each month against a data extract that is overwritten in place. A drop in performance is noticed in the current version, and the team wants to compare it against the extract used two versions ago. That extract no longer exists. What should the project manager put in place?
option_a: More frequent retraining, so any drop in performance is detected sooner after it begins
option_b: A record of the row count of each extract, so changes in volume can be identified
option_c: Approval from the data owner before each monthly extract replaces the previous one
option_d: Retention of each data extract alongside the model version trained on it
explanation: Investigating a change in model behaviour requires the data of each version, not only its code.
explanation_a: Earlier detection is useful but does not help with diagnosis. The team would still lack the data needed to explain what changed.
explanation_b: Volume is one signal among many and would not reveal a shift in the content of the records. It is far short of retaining the extract.
explanation_c: An approval step adds governance to the overwrite without preventing the loss. The extract would still be gone.
explanation_d: A change in results comes from the model, the data or both. Without the earlier extract the two cannot be separated, and the investigation has nowhere to start.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A lending organisation must be able to tell a declined applicant which factors drove the decision. The data science team proposes an ensemble that scores several points higher on the validation set than a simpler alternative, but cannot attribute an individual decision to specific inputs. What should the project manager conclude?
option_a: Validation performance should decide it, since the simpler model scores lower
option_b: Explainability is a requirement the model must meet, not a preference traded against accuracy
option_c: Approve the ensemble and have staff write plain-language decline letters afterwards
option_d: Retrain the ensemble on a larger sample so its behaviour becomes clear enough to explain
explanation: A constraint the solution must satisfy is not a criterion to be traded off against model performance.
explanation_a: Objective measurement makes validation performance comparable between candidates, but it does not make it the only criterion. A model that cannot meet a stated requirement is not selectable on score alone.
explanation_b: The organisation is obliged to give applicants the factors behind a decision, so a model that cannot supply them fails a requirement. A higher validation score does not substitute for meeting it.
explanation_c: A letter written after the fact can describe the outcome but not the factors behind it, because the ensemble cannot attribute a decision to specific inputs. The requirement would remain unmet.
explanation_d: More training data may change what the ensemble predicts, but it does not change whether the method can attribute a prediction to particular inputs. The limitation is structural, not a matter of sample size.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: Two candidate models for an equipment failure warning system reach the same overall accuracy on the same test set. Model A misses more genuine failures but raises few false alarms. Model B catches nearly every failure but raises many false alarms. An unplanned failure halts a production line for a full shift, while a false alarm results only in a short inspection that does not interrupt production. Which model should be preferred?
option_a: Model A, because frequent false alarms will cause staff to lose confidence in the system
option_b: Model B, because a missed failure costs far more here than a false alarm
option_c: Either model, since their equal accuracy shows they perform equivalently on this problem
option_d: Neither, until a third model is built that reduces both kinds of error simultaneously
explanation: Equal accuracy can conceal very different error mixes, and the costlier error decides between them.
explanation_a: Alarm fatigue is a genuine risk, managed through how alerts are presented and triaged. Against a stem in which an inspection does not interrupt production, it does not outweigh a shift of lost output per missed failure.
explanation_b: A halted line for a shift dwarfs the cost of an unnecessary inspection. With accuracy equal, the model that errs towards the cheaper mistake is the better choice.
explanation_c: Equal accuracy means the total number of errors matches. It says nothing about which errors were made, which is what determines the cost here.
explanation_d: Seeking a better model is reasonable in principle but defers a decision that the evidence already supports. The choice between the two is clear on cost.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A model that assesses loan applications performs well across the applicant population overall. The project manager finds that on applications from newly established businesses, which are few in the data but are a stated growth segment, its performance is substantially worse. How should this be treated?
option_a: As expected behaviour, since a segment with few records will always be predicted less accurately
option_b: As a data quality problem, since the records for the segment are evidently unreliable
option_c: As a matter for monitoring after deployment, once more applications from the segment accumulate
option_d: As a material gap, since the segment matters to the business regardless of its size in the data
explanation: Aggregate performance can be acceptable while a segment the business depends on is served badly.
explanation_a: Fewer records often does mean weaker performance, but treating that as acceptable leaves a stated priority unserved. It explains the gap rather than resolving it.
explanation_b: Nothing indicates the records are unreliable. Scarcity and unreliability are different problems with different remedies.
explanation_c: Deferring leaves the segment poorly served in the meantime. It should be understood before launch, not after.
explanation_d: The aggregate figure is dominated by the common case. A segment the organisation intends to grow needs to be evaluated and accepted on its own performance.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team building a model to predict whether a service request will breach its response deadline includes a field recording the number of escalation calls logged against the request. The team confirms that an escalation call is logged only once a breach has already been recorded. What should the project manager conclude about this feature?
option_a: It records what happened after the outcome, so it will not be available when the prediction is needed
option_b: It should be retained, because the strength of its relationship with the outcome is clearly established
option_c: It should be retained but given a lower weight, so the model does not depend on it too heavily
option_d: It should be retained and the escalation calls logged earlier, so the field is populated before any breach
explanation: A feature recorded after the outcome cannot be available at the moment the prediction must be made.
explanation_a: The model is meant to give warning before a breach. A field populated only after a breach is recorded cannot be present at the moment the prediction is required, so its strength in testing will not carry into use.
explanation_b: The relationship is strong precisely because the field follows the outcome. Strength in the training data is what makes this feature misleading rather than what justifies it.
explanation_c: Reducing the weight does not make the field available at prediction time. The feature would still be absent when the model is asked to run.
explanation_d: Changing when staff log calls is a process change outside the model's control, and it would alter what the field means. It does not address the present feature.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team assembling a feature set for a model with about four hundred training records has produced over two hundred candidate features by combining fields in many ways. The team argues that the model can simply ignore whichever features do not help. What should the project manager raise?
option_a: Combine fields in still more ways, so predictive features are not missed
option_b: Two hundred features will take too long to compute when scoring each new record
option_c: With this many features and so few records, the model can fit relationships that do not generalise
option_d: Features built by combining fields cannot be interpreted or described afterwards
explanation: With few records relative to features, a model can find patterns that hold only in the training data.
explanation_a: Adding candidates makes the imbalance between features and records worse. It increases the number of chance relationships rather than improving the chance of finding real ones.
explanation_b: Computation time for a few hundred features is a performance concern rather than a modelling one, and it is not what makes this feature set risky. The statistical problem is the more serious issue.
explanation_c: With many candidate features relative to the number of records, there are more opportunities to fit relationships that arise by chance, which increases overfitting risk and weakens generalisation.
explanation_d: Derived features can be described in terms of the fields they combine. Interpretability is a real consideration but is not the central risk here.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team has trained a model that flags invoices for manual review before payment. The team asks which measures should be reported to the finance stakeholders, who care about the money lost to incorrect payments and about the reviewer hours the process will consume. Select two.
option_a: The overall share of invoices the model classifies correctly
option_b: The share of incorrect invoices the model flags
option_c: The total value of the incorrect invoices the model fails to flag
option_d: The time the model takes to score a single invoice
explanation: Reported measures have to be expressed in the units the stakeholders are accountable for.
explanation_a: Overall accuracy counts correct classifications rather than the monetary value of missed incorrect invoices or the review workload created by flagged invoices. It therefore does not directly measure either stakeholder concern.
explanation_b: This counts cases rather than value. Where incorrect invoices differ in amount, the share flagged does not establish how much money escapes detection, which is what the stakeholders asked about.
explanation_c: Incorrect invoices vary in value, so a count of them does not measure the loss. Totalling the value of those that escape detection expresses the first concern in the unit the stakeholders are accountable for.
explanation_d: Scoring speed matters for system design if volumes are high. It is not one of the two outcomes the stakeholders have raised.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
option_e: The volume of invoices flagged for review, together with the effort each review takes
explanation_e: Reviewer hours follow from how many invoices are sent for review and how long each one takes. Flagged volume combined with review effort gives the workload the stakeholders must staff.

question: A gaming company cannot license additional images, as the rights holder has declined further use. Its permitted use of the images it holds covers making modified copies for training, and the team has confirmed that the transformations it proposes leave each image's class unchanged. The team must enlarge the training set from the images the company already holds. Which approach fits that constraint?
option_a: Generate variants of existing images through transformations such as rotation and crop
option_b: Duplicate the existing images so that each one appears several times in training
option_c: Collect supplementary images from public websites without reviewing the terms attached to them
option_d: Reduce the resolution of existing images so that more of them fit into memory
explanation: Augmentation adds variation the model can learn from; copying adds none.
explanation_a: Transformations the team has confirmed to be class-preserving produce genuinely different inputs that still carry the same label. The model sees more variation in how the subject can appear, within the permitted use the stem establishes.
explanation_b: Duplicates add rows without adding information. The model sees the same examples more often, which encourages memorisation rather than better generalisation.
explanation_c: Scraping without checking terms substitutes one licensing problem for a larger one, and the company has already stated it cannot license more images.
explanation_d: Lower resolution fits more images in memory but does not create additional images, and it discards detail the classifier may depend on.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
topic: Training data strategy and validation design

question: A model is trained to predict which employees will be promoted, using ten years of the organisation's promotion records as the outcome to learn from. The project manager is told the outcome is objective because it records what actually happened. What is the flaw in that reasoning?
option_a: The records capture past promotion decisions, along with whatever shaped them
option_b: Ten years is too long a period, because promotion criteria will have changed over that time
option_c: Promotion records are administrative data and will contain entry errors and omissions
option_d: The model should predict performance ratings instead, as these are assessed against fixed criteria
explanation: A recorded outcome reflects the decisions that produced it, including any patterns in how they were made.
explanation_a: The model learns to reproduce how promotions were awarded, not who merited them. Any pattern in the historical decisions is carried forward as the standard to match.
explanation_b: Shifting criteria are worth examining and may argue for a shorter window. That is a separate issue from what the outcome field represents.
explanation_c: Recording errors are a data quality matter to be assessed. They are not the reason an accurate promotion record is a questionable target.
explanation_d: Performance ratings are also assigned by people and carry the same kind of imprint. Substituting them does not resolve the problem.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A model has met its agreed performance level and the team proposes moving to deployment. The project manager is asked to confirm that the deployment decision is properly evidenced. Beyond the headline score, what should the evaluation record contain?
option_a: The full history of every experiment the team ran while developing the model
option_b: The computing resources the model will require to score records in production
option_c: The model's error patterns, the population evaluated and the conditions it was not tested under
option_d: A statement that the model met the agreed level, signed off by the team that built it
explanation: A deployment decision rests on how a model fails and where it applies, not on a single score.
explanation_a: A complete experiment history supports reproducibility and is worth retaining. It is not what the deployment decision turns on.
explanation_b: Infrastructure sizing is needed for the deployment plan. It speaks to running the model rather than to whether it should be run.
explanation_c: Whoever operates the model needs to know how it fails, for whom it was shown to work and where evidence is absent. A single score answers none of those.
explanation_d: Sign-off records agreement with the headline figure. It adds a signature rather than the evidence behind the decision.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team selects the algorithm that scored highest during model selection. The project manager notes that a substantial share of incoming records arrive with one or more fields absent, and that the selected algorithm produces no output at all for a record with a missing field. What should the project manager require?
option_a: That the records with absent fields be excluded from scoring once the model is in use
option_b: That candidates be compared on records that include the absent fields the model will receive
option_c: That the selected algorithm be retrained on a larger sample so it tolerates absent fields
option_d: That the absent fields be dropped from the feature set so every record can be scored
explanation: A model is selectable only if it can produce an output for the records it will actually be given.
explanation_a: Excluding those records leaves a substantial share of cases without a prediction, which is the outcome the model was meant to provide. It converts a modelling gap into a coverage gap.
explanation_b: The selection compared candidates on records that do not resemble what will arrive. Comparing them on records carrying the same absences establishes which candidate can actually serve the incoming data.
explanation_c: More training records do not give an algorithm the ability to accept an input it cannot process. The limitation is in what the method accepts, not in how much it has seen.
