explanation_d: Dropping every field that is sometimes absent can remove much of the model's predictive information, and it addresses the input shape rather than which candidate suits the data.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A model screens medical images for a condition that is treatable when caught early and serious when missed. Flagged images go to a specialist for a second look. The team has tuned the model to the cut-off that maximises overall accuracy. What should the project manager challenge?
option_a: That the cut-off should have been chosen before the model was trained rather than after
option_b: That accuracy cannot be calculated at all for a model that produces a continuous score
option_c: That the specialist review step should be removed so the model's decisions stand on their own
option_d: That the two errors are being treated as equally costly when they clearly are not
explanation: Maximising accuracy treats each misclassification equally, which can be inappropriate when the two errors differ in consequence.
explanation_a: The cut-off is normally set once scores exist, and doing so afterwards is standard. The objection is which criterion was used to set it.
explanation_b: Accuracy is readily calculated once a cut-off converts scores into decisions. The measure is available; it is simply the wrong one to optimise here.
explanation_c: Removing human review would raise the cost of every error rather than reduce it. It makes the underlying problem worse.
explanation_d: Maximising accuracy weighs a missed condition the same as an unnecessary specialist review. The scenario establishes that a miss risks serious harm while a false flag costs a review, so the cut-off should reflect that difference.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A model has been evaluated on held-out records drawn from the twelve sites where it was trained. The planned rollout covers those twelve sites and nine further sites that contributed no data. The team presents the held-out score as evidence the model is ready. What should the project manager require before the rollout is approved?
option_a: A larger held-out set drawn from the twelve sites, so the reported score is more precise
option_b: Confirmation that the nine further sites use the same recording systems as the original twelve
option_c: Evidence of performance at sites that contributed no data, before those sites are included
option_d: A commitment to re-evaluate the model at the nine further sites once the rollout is complete
explanation: Evaluation evidence covers the population it was drawn from, not the wider population of a rollout.
explanation_a: A larger sample from the same twelve sites sharpens an estimate for those sites. It says nothing about the nine that contributed no data.
explanation_b: Matching recording systems would remove one source of difference and is worth confirming. Sites can still differ in case mix and local practice, so it does not establish performance at the new sites.
explanation_c: The held-out score describes the twelve sites it was drawn from. Extending the rollout to sites outside that population needs evidence for those sites, whether from a pilot, a held-out site or comparable data.
explanation_d: Re-evaluating after the rollout means the nine sites operate on unevidenced performance in the interim, which is what the approval decision is meant to prevent.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A project manager reviews the feature set assembled for a shipping cost model and finds two numeric fields, one recording package weight in pounds and the other recording the same weight in kilograms, so that each is an exact conversion of the other. What is the practical consequence of keeping both?
option_a: The pair will cause the training process to fail with a conversion error
option_b: The pair will double the storage the feature set requires in the warehouse
option_c: The pair will prevent the dataset from being split into training and test sets
option_d: The pair adds no information and can complicate interpretation of the model
explanation: Two expressions of one measurement are one feature written twice.
explanation_a: Training runs perfectly well with correlated features. No conversion error arises from having both units present.
explanation_b: One extra numeric column is a negligible storage cost. Efficiency is not the meaningful consequence.
explanation_c: Splitting is unaffected by feature redundancy. The split operates on rows, not on the relationship between columns.
explanation_d: The second field carries nothing the first does not. Redundant representations can also complicate or divide feature-attribution measures, depending on the model and the interpretation method used.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: Two models are compared for a triage tool that will rank incoming cases so reviewers work through the highest-risk first. Model A scores higher on accuracy at the default cut-off; model B separates high-risk from low-risk cases better across all cut-offs. The cut-off has not yet been fixed. Which model should be preferred?
option_a: Model A, because accuracy at the default cut-off is the measure the stakeholders will recognise
option_b: Model B, because the tool depends on ranking and the cut-off can still be chosen
option_c: Model A, because a model that is more accurate at one cut-off will be more accurate at any other
option_d: Neither, until both models have been retrained on the same data with the same cut-off applied
explanation: Where the operating point is not yet fixed, ranking quality matters more than accuracy at one cut-off.
explanation_a: Familiarity is a reason to explain a measure carefully, not to select on it. The default cut-off is arbitrary and will not be the one the tool uses.
explanation_b: The reviewers work down an ordered list, so what matters is whether risky cases sit above safe ones. A model that ranks better will outperform once the cut-off is set appropriately.
explanation_c: This does not follow. Two models can cross, so ordering at one cut-off does not determine the ordering elsewhere.
explanation_d: The models are already being compared on the same data. Fixing a single cut-off first would discard the ranking evidence that distinguishes them.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team has around three hundred labelled records for a specialised classification problem and no prospect of obtaining more. Setting aside a fifth of them for testing leaves the model with little to learn from, and the resulting score swings widely depending on which records are held out. What approach addresses this?
option_a: Reduce the held-out portion to a twentieth so more records remain available for training
option_b: Repeat the single split several times and report whichever result is closest to the average
option_c: Train on all three hundred records and report the accuracy measured on those same records
option_d: Cross-validation, rotating the held-out portion across several rounds and averaging the results
explanation: Rotating which records are held out uses every record for both training and testing across repeated rounds.
explanation_a: A smaller test set leaves more for training but makes the score even less stable, because it now rests on fifteen records. This worsens the swing rather than addressing it.
explanation_b: Selecting a result because it looks typical discards the evidence of variation. The spread is information about reliability, not noise to be filtered out.
explanation_c: A score measured on the training records reflects what the model has memorised. It gives no indication of behaviour on records the model has not seen.
explanation_d: Every record serves as training data in some rounds and as test data in others. The averaged score rests on all the data and is far less sensitive to one unlucky split.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
topic: Training data strategy and validation design

question: A recruitment screening model is reported at eighty-four per cent accuracy overall. The project manager asks for results broken down by applicant group and finds the model rejects qualified applicants far more often in one group than in others. The team says the overall figure meets the agreed target. What should the project manager conclude?
option_a: Meeting an aggregate target does not establish that the model performs acceptably for each group
option_b: The breakdown is not comparable, because the groups contain different numbers of applicants
option_c: The difference is acceptable provided the model was not given the group as an input
option_d: The model should be retrained until every group reaches exactly the same error rate
explanation: One aggregate figure cannot show whether a model's errors fall evenly across the people it affects.
explanation_a: An overall figure averages across groups, so strong performance on large groups can conceal poor performance on smaller ones. The agreed target does not test that distribution.
explanation_b: Error rates are proportions, so they remain comparable across groups of different sizes. Small groups give less precise estimates, which is a reason to check precision rather than dismiss the finding.
explanation_c: Excluding an attribute does not prevent a model from producing different error rates across groups, as other fields can carry the same information.
explanation_d: Exact equality is not automatically the appropriate fairness criterion. The criterion has to be defined for this use, and the observed disparity investigated against it.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: Before evaluation begins, the project manager wants the criteria for proceeding to deployment agreed in advance rather than debated once results are in. The team asks what those criteria should specify. Select two.
option_a: The algorithm the team intends to use to build the model
option_b: The minimum performance the model must reach on the measure that matters to the business
option_c: The number of experiments the team expects to run before reaching the target
option_d: The date on which the deployment decision will be taken
explanation: Criteria fixed before results are seen prevent the standard being adjusted to fit the outcome.
explanation_a: Fixing the method in advance constrains the work without making the decision testable. The criteria concern the result, not the route to it.
explanation_b: A stated level on an agreed measure is what makes the result testable. Without it, any outcome can be argued as sufficient once it is known.
explanation_c: Experiment count is a planning estimate. It says nothing about whether the resulting model is good enough to deploy.
explanation_d: A date sets the timetable for the decision but supplies no standard against which to take it.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
option_e: The data the model must reach that level on
explanation_e: A level is meaningless without the data it applies to. Naming the evaluation set in advance prevents a favourable set being chosen afterwards.

question: A team is preparing features for a model that predicts insurance claim handling time. Profiling shows the handling-office code field contains several thousand distinct values, and that the large majority of those codes appear in only a few claims each. What issue does this raise for feature preparation?
option_a: The field will consume substantially more storage than all other features combined
option_b: The field cannot be used at all because models accept only numeric input values
option_c: The field will need sorting into alphabetical order before it can serve as a feature
option_d: Sparse categories make category-specific patterns hard to estimate reliably
explanation: High cardinality spreads the data thin, leaving most categories with almost no examples.
explanation_a: Storage for one identifier column is negligible. Cost is not what makes high cardinality difficult to work with.
explanation_b: Categorical fields can be encoded into numeric representations. The need to encode applies to every category field, not uniquely to this one.
explanation_c: Sorting affects presentation and some join strategies. It has no bearing on how a model consumes a categorical feature.
explanation_d: With several thousand offices, most appear in only a handful of claims, leaving little evidence for category-specific behaviour. This needs deliberate treatment such as grouping, encoding choices or regularisation rather than naive use of the raw codes.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation

question: A team is building an intrusion detection model on network logs in which roughly 0.1% of events are genuine attacks. An early model is reported to the project manager as achieving 99.9% accuracy on the held-out test set, and the team proposes moving to the next phase. What should the project manager conclude about the reported performance?
option_a: The dataset is of unusually high quality given the accuracy achieved
option_b: The dataset needs additional features to push accuracy above 99.9%
option_c: The dataset should be split differently to raise the measured accuracy
option_d: The severe class imbalance makes overall accuracy uninformative, so performance on the attack class must be examined separately
explanation: At a base rate this extreme, predicting the majority class alone scores near-perfect accuracy.
explanation_a: Reading the figure as evidence of data quality is the trap the imbalance sets. The number reflects the class distribution rather than the dataset or the model.
explanation_b: Chasing a higher number on a metric that cannot discriminate here compounds the error. More features do not make overall accuracy informative about the attack class.
explanation_c: Changing the split shifts which records land where without altering the base rate. The metric would remain equally uninformative.
explanation_d: A model labelling every event as normal reaches 99.9% while catching no intrusions. Overall accuracy alone is therefore uninformative about attack-class detection at this level of imbalance, so performance on the attack class has to be measured in its own right.
domain: Manage AI Model Development and Evaluation
